description: Hey everyone, we’re MicroVibe, a team of three tackling Flame in Freefall. We’re building an AI-powered dashboard that makes decades of NASA microgravity fire data searchable and useful for Moon and Mars safety.
summary:
FireSight is an interactive, SI-powered dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion archive into fire-safety answers for Moon and Mars habitats. We extracted 772 real test runs from 20 NASA investigations. 764 come from Physical Science Informatics tables (BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, CFI, Saffire I–III) and 8 come from published Saffire IV–VI papers. Every value links back to its source file and row, and nothing is synthetic.

You pick a cabin atmosphere, such as ISS, lunar base or Mars transit. FireSight then shows which real experiments tested fuels at or near that air, what happened, and what has never been tested. It ranks investigations by relevance with a score you can adjust, and the SI interprets each condition, citing run IDs. Other pages show what crews did to put flames out, compare oxygen levels during a fire, answer plain-English questions about the data, and plan the next experiments to close the gaps.

This matters because exploration cabins will run at lower pressure and higher oxygen. Of the 268 solid-fuel runs with a known oxygen level, 262 were at ordinary cabin air. FireSight makes that gap visible and helps decide what NASA should test next.
details:
What it does

FireSight is a web dashboard that answers one question for future Moon and Mars habitats: has anyone actually tested fire in this air? It has seven pages.

  • Habitat Flammability Explorer (main feature): Pick a cabin atmosphere by preset or with oxygen and pressure sliders. FireSight gives a coverage verdict for solid, liquid and gas fuels (Tested, Near tested runs, Not tested) and plots a 144-square coverage map. It lists the five nearest real runs with their results and sources. Its SI explanation cites run IDs. A "Fire Twin" cabin simulation decides which items can ignite from real runs; its spread timings are labelled as illustrative. An oxygen comparison asks whether lowering the oxygen during a fire would help, using real-run counts at both levels and showing what the crew would breathe.
  • Crew Response Evidence: 75 crew actions, such as turning the fans off or using a nitrogen jet, hand-coded from BASS investigator notes, with how often each one put the flame out. Each action keeps the investigator's exact words.
  • Experiment Planner: A greedy search places a budget of new tests where they close the most untested ground between existing runs and mission atmospheres. The SI writes a cited proposal you can export.
  • Investigation Explorer, Ask the Data and Back on Earth: Search and compare all 20 investigations, ask questions answered only from retrieved records, and see each one's benefits on Earth.

How it works

We downloaded NASA PSI experiment tables and wrote one extractor per dataset. That gave 772 run-level tests: 764 from PSI and 8 transcribed from Saffire IV–VI papers. Every value carries its source file and row. Missing values stay missing. A build step checks the data and refuses to build if any check fails, covering unit conversions, provenance and outcome sources.

All verdicts, distances and rankings are computed in TypeScript. The SI only explains numbers it is given, its answers are validated, and it may cite only IDs it received.

Benefits and impact

Exploration cabins are planned at lower pressure and higher oxygen, where materials burn more easily. The data shows that 262 of 268 solid-fuel runs with a known oxygen level were tested at ordinary cabin air. FireSight makes that gap visible in seconds. It helps engineers, researchers and students find the closest real evidence for any cabin, see what crews did that worked, and decide which experiment NASA should fly next.

Tools

TypeScript, Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, TanStack Table, zod, fuse.js, the OpenAI API (server-side only, with responses cached), Vitest (139 tests) and Vercel hosting. No special hardware was used.

What makes it creative

  • It shows where the evidence ends instead of a confident risk score.
  • The Fire Twin turns dry tables into a fire you can watch, and marks what is data and what is illustrative.
  • The planner turns the gaps into a concrete flight campaign.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: we use only real data, with no synthetic fill-ins.
  • Traceability: every number links back to its NASA source.
  • The limits of the data: every run was in microgravity, many outcomes are not stated, and BASS-II records no pressure (we place it at the cited ISS 14.7 psi and mark it).
  • Avoiding overclaiming: the one statistical flame estimate is labelled "Estimate, not a test". FireSight does not replace NASA flammability standards.
  • Plain language for non-experts.
  • Reproducibility and open source under the MIT licence.
